newsitem.title: USA: Aetna stock jumps after Q3 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Aetna stock jumps after Q3 earnings.

text.p: Aetna Inc's stock rose more than three points on Friday, defying uncertainty elsewhere in the HMO industry by meeting analysts' expectations for third quarter earnings.

The jump in the stock price was fueled in large part by confidence in Aetna's efforts to concentrate on health insurance, analysts said, as the company shed its property and casualty insurance segments.
The company's third quarter earnings, which included results from newly acquired U.S. Healthcare, were essentially in line with analysts' estimates.

Conning & Co analyst Paul Goulekas attributed the jump in the stock, up 3-3/4 to 63-7/8 by mid-afternoon, to two factors: Aetna's holding steady in an uncertain industry and the company's possible stock buyback program.
"People are very worried about HMO results in general, and there were some people out there who expected they'd do worse than they did," Goulekas said.

Another possible factor, he said, is that Aetna executives speaking to analysts on Friday suggested there could be a share repurchase program, which could raise the stock price. Aetna did not promise such a program would occur and did not offer any possible level, he said.
Aetna spokeswoman Joyce Oberdorf declined to confirm or deny the possibility of a share buyback.
For the third quarter, Aetna reported net income of $122.4 million, or $0.77 per share, compared to $212.1 million, or $0.98 per share.
However, when an after-tax restructuring charge of $31.8 million is excluded, earnings for the period came in at $0.95 per share, which is in line with analysts' estimates.
"They met expectations," said Tom Hodapp, an analyst with Robertson Stephens & Co. "It's still fairly early to see how successful they will be in the transition to managed care."
"If nothing else, people are impressed they are making a go of it," he added. "It still is an execution game."

Among the determining factors are pharmacy costs, which account for between 12 percent and 15 percent of Aetna's expenses. According to Hodapp, Aetna executives said they intend to find ways to cut pharmacy costs.
Although that area is not the most significant, "it's by far the most difficult to control and it's inflating," Hodapp said.

The company told analysts that its pharmacy contracts are more favorable than those held by U.S. Healthcare. So there are plans to convert the U.S. Healthcare contracts to Aetna's where there are overlaps, he said.
